rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the trees drink the same water from below, it reaches their branching upper limbs.
rows.anchor: لأنه يشرب من أسفله فيصل الماء إلى فروعه المتشعبة من أعلاه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The differentiation is in the fruit and what is eaten.
rows.anchor: «ونفضل بعضها على بعض في الأكل» (4) فى الثمرة والأكل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aghlāl is plural of ghull, which is only a neck collar.
rows.anchor: واحدها غل لا يكون إلا فى العنق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathulāt is plural of mathula, and its expression is likened to amthāl.
rows.anchor: واحدتها مثلة ومجازها مجاز الأمثال.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What wombs diminish includes the children and whatever was inside them that they release.
rows.anchor: أي ما تخرج من الأولاد ومما كان فيها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What wombs increase is what develops or comes about in them.
rows.anchor: «وما تزداد» (8) أي ما تحدث وتحدث.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everything with God is measured; miqdār is on the mifʿāl pattern from qadr.
rows.anchor: أي مقدر وهو مفعال من القدر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sārib means one travelling through his routes and directions; being safe in one's sarb means safe wherever one turns.
rows.anchor: مجازه: سالك فى سربه، أي مذاهبه ووجوهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guardians are angels succeeding one another, with night guards following day guards and day guards following night guards; Arabic idiom uses ʿaqaba for following.
rows.anchor: ملائكة تعقب بعد ملائكة، وحفظة تعقب بالليل حفظة النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They protect him by God's command from His command.
rows.anchor: أي بأمر الله يحفظونه من أمره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With initial ḍamma, sūʾ means calamity, including ruin, disease, blindness, or any great affliction; with initial fatḥa it is the verbal noun of doing evil to people.
rows.anchor: مضموم الأول، ومجازه: هلكة وكل جذام وبرص وعمى، وكل بلاء عظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zibriqān ibn Badr's line uses al-sūʾ for an enemy fighter, illustrating the word's usage.
rows.anchor: وقيت إذا ما فارس السوء أحجما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lightning makes people fear while hoping that God will revive and give them rain.
rows.anchor: أي ترهبونه وتطمعون أن يحييكم وأن يغيثكم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yunshiʾ means to begin; one says nas ha when a cloud begins.
rows.anchor: أي يبدأ السحاب، ويقال: إذا بدأ «نشأ» .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation makes al-raʿd an angel appointed over thunder; the cited reference to angels fearing God supports this view.
rows.anchor: إما أن يكون اسم ملك قد وكل بالرعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes al-raʿd as the cloud's sound, supported by the cited phrase about angels fearing God.
rows.anchor: وإما أن يكون صوت سحاب واحتجوا بآخر الكلام: «والملائكة من خيفته»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An Arab line calls thunder's voice rough, supporting the interpretation of al-raʿd as sound.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون هكذا إلا الصوت.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To repel evil with good means to drive the evil away by means of good.
rows.anchor: أي يدفعون السيئة بالحسنة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUqbā al-dār means the outcome of the abode.
rows.anchor: «عقبى الدار» (24) عاقبة الدار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salāmun ʿalaykum is an abbreviated clause with an understood subject, as in “they say: peace be upon you.”
rows.anchor: مجازه مجاز المختصر الذي فيه ضمير كقولك: يقولون سلام عليكم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present life compared with the Hereafter is only a brief, trifling possession.
rows.anchor: إلا متعة وشىء طفيف حقير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One who turns back to God is one who repents.
rows.anchor: «من أناب» (27) من تاب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭūbā and a good return describe a good destination or return.
rows.anchor: «طوبى لهم وحسن مآب» (29) أي منقلب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Communities and generations had passed before the community addressed.
rows.anchor: أي مضت قرون من قبلها وملل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Matāb is the verbal noun of turning back to God, equivalent to saying “my repentance is to Him.”
rows.anchor: مصدر تبت إليه، وتوبتى إليه سواء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional sentence is left without its result, then resumed with “rather, the whole command belongs to God”; the understood result is that the mountains would move, the earth split, and the dead rise. Arabs omit a predictable result for economy.
rows.anchor: مجازُه مجاز المكفوف عن خبره، ثم استؤنف فقال: «بل لله الأمر جميعا» (31)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Akhtal's final-line construction illustrates an omitted, understood result in Arabic poetry.
rows.anchor: خلا أن حيا من قريش تفضلوا ... على الناس أو أن الأكارم نهشلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending of ʿAbd Manāf ibn Rubʿ al-Hudhalī's poem likewise stops before an understood result, illustrating the ellipsis.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا اسلكوهم فى قتائدة ... شلا كما تطرد الجمالة الشردا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Livestock provide warmth from their wool and other benefits besides warmth.
rows.anchor: أي ما استدفئ به من أوبارها. ومنافع سوى ذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Returning livestock is in the evening; sending them out to graze is in the morning.
rows.anchor: بالعشي «وحين تسرحون» (6) بالغداة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial shīn in bi-shaqq al-anfus may be read with either kasra or fatḥa; both forms mean with the souls' hardship.
rows.anchor: يكسر أوله ويفتح ومعناه بمشقة الأنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Namir ibn Tawlab uses shiq for hardship in his line about the burden of camels.
rows.anchor: وذى إبل يسعى ويحسبها له ... أخى نصب من شقها ودؤوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj's phrase shiqan also means hardship, as in undergoing difficulty.
rows.anchor:
أصبح مسحول يوازى شقا
أي يقاسى مشقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabīl has singular form but collective meaning here, as though one path among paths were crooked; some Arabs treat sabīl as feminine.
rows.anchor: السبيل: لفظه لفظ الواحد، وهو فى موضع الجميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasīmūn means grazing: one can say camels are pastured or that they graze themselves.
rows.anchor: يقال: أسمت إبلى وسامت هى، أي رعيتها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dharʾ means to create.
rows.anchor: «وما ذرأ لكم» (13) أي ما خلق لكم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawākir describes ships cutting the water with their prows; fulk is grammatically singular in form but collective in sense, hence its plural-like adjective fawāʿil.
rows.anchor: من مخرت الماء أي شقته بجآجئها، والفلك هاهنا فى موضع جميع فقال فواعل، وهو موضع واحد كقوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭā Hā functions like the disconnected letters opening other sūrahs, with the same introductory function.
rows.anchor: ساكن لأنه جرى مجرى فواتح سائر السور اللواتى مجازهن مجاز حروف التهجي ومجاز موضعه فى المعنى كمجاز ابتداء فواتح سائر السور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ṭufayla al-Ḥaramazī claims that Ṭā Hā means “O man.”
rows.anchor: فزعم أن طه «يا رجل»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda rejects treating Ṭā Hā as a name because it is indeclinable in this explanation; a name would take case inflection.
rows.anchor: ولا ينبغى أن يكون اسما لأنه ساكن ولو كان اسما لدخله الإعراب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse uses fronting and postponement with an understood pronoun; it can mean the Qur'an was sent down as a reminder for the God-fearing, not to cause hardship, or that a reminder was sent down separately from the hardship clause.
rows.anchor: مجازُه مجاز المقدم والمؤخر وفيه ضمير، وله موضع آخر من المختصر الذي فيه ضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istawā means rose or ascended above; Arabic uses it of rising over a mount, camel, mountain, or house.
rows.anchor: أي علا، يقال: استويت فوق الدابة وعلى البعير وعلى الجبل وفوق البيت، أي علوت عليه وفوقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān may be nominative by detaching it from the preceding genitive and beginning anew.
rows.anchor: ورفع الرحمن فى مكانين: أحدهما على القطع من الأول المجرور والابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, its nominative is analyzed through the verb: “The Merciful rose over the Throne.”
rows.anchor: وعلى إعمال الفعل، مجازه: استوى الرحمن على العرش.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naquṣṣu means “we recount” or “narrate it to you.”
rows.anchor: «كذلك نقص عليك» (99) مجازه نأثره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wizr is a weight, load, or sin; the phrase in verse 101 refers back to that burden.
rows.anchor: «فإنه يحمل يوم القيامة وزرا» (100) أي ثقلا وحملا وإثما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden is what they carry on the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: «خالدين فيه وساء لهم» (101) ذلك الوزر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden is what they carry on the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ذلك الوزر «يوم القيامة حملا» (101) ..

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They whisper secretly to one another; the related wording in 17:110 also means lowering one's voice.
rows.anchor: يتسارون ويهمس بعضهم إلى بعض بالكلام وفى آية أخرى: «ولا تخافت بها» (17/ 110)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yansifu means that God makes the mountains fly away and removes them completely.
rows.anchor: «ويسئلونك عن الجبال فقل ينسفها ربي نسفا» (105) مجازها: يطيرها فيستأصلها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāʿan ṣafṣafā describes level, smooth ground.
rows.anchor: «فيذرها قاعا صفصفا» (106) أي مستويا أملس.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With initial kasra, ʿiwaj is the verbal noun for bends in paths, streams, valleys, or uneven rises to either side; with initial fatḥa it applies to upright things such as a spear, tooth, or wall.
rows.anchor: مجازه مصدر ما اعوج من المحانى والمسايل والأودية والارتفاع يمينا وشمالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amt means no rise or depression; usage includes rope with no slack and a waterskin with no bulge, as in lines by Yazīd ibn Ḍabba and an unnamed rajaz poet.
rows.anchor: مجازه لا ربى ولا وطئا أي لا ارتفاع ولا هبوط، يقال: مد حبله حتى ما ترك فيه أمتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yazīd ibn Ḍabba's line uses amt for an unevenness absent from a woman described as smooth and white.
rows.anchor: منعمة بيضاء ليس بها أمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed rajaz poet uses amt for an irregularity in the drawing or movement of a rope.
rows.anchor: ما فى انجذاب سيره من أمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hams is a faint, hidden sound like al-rakz; to whisper something to someone is to conceal it.
rows.anchor: أي صوتا خفيا وهو مثل الركز، ويقال: همس إلى بحديث، أي أخفاه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faces become subdued and captive before the Ever-Living Sustainer; ʿanā means to become a captive, and an ʿānī is like a humbled prisoner.
rows.anchor: فهى تعنو عنوا أي استأسرت فهى عوان لربها، واحدها عان بمنزلة الأسير العاني لأسره، أي ذليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom “women are captives with their husbands” illustrates ʿawān as a captive or subdued person.
rows.anchor: ومنه قولهم: النساء عوان عند أزواجهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “whoever does good deeds,” min is an extra particle; Arabic also adds it in non-assertive settings, especially after negation, as in 69:47 and a cited poem, but not in a positive assertion.
rows.anchor: من حروف الزوائد، وفى آية أخرى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rule is that min may be added after negation or a question, but not in a positive assertion such as “I have a dirham.”
rows.anchor: زاد «من» لمكان النفي ولا تزاد «من» فى أمر واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's phrase “from anyone before me” exemplifies min after negation.
rows.anchor: جزيتك ضعف الحب لما استثبته ... وما إن جزاك الضعف من أحد قبلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-qāniʿ is a supplicant who comes to ask humbly; its verbal noun is qunūʿ, and al-Shammākh's use of al-qunūʿ illustrates asking and need.
rows.anchor: مجازه السائل الذي قنع إليكم تقدير فعله: ذهب يذهب ومعناه سأل وخضع ومصدره القنوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shammākh uses qunūʿ for poverty, asking, and humility in the phrase contrasting it with a person's wealth.
rows.anchor: لمال المرء يصلحه فيغنى ... مفاقره أعف من القنوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muʿtarr is a visitor who approaches and comes to you expecting a gift; the author lists several forms of the verb for visiting.
rows.anchor: والمعتر الذي يعتريك يأتيك لتعطيه تقول: اعترنى وعرنى واعتريته واعتقيته إذا ألممت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥassān's line says the muʿtarr comes to their land, illustrating the visiting sense.
rows.anchor: لعمرك ما المعتر يأتى بلادنا ... لنمنعه بالضائع المتهضم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-qāniʿ can instead mean someone content and satisfied; qanaʿa with the relevant noun forms describes satisfaction, distinct from the supplicant's qunūʿ.
rows.anchor: وأما القانع فى معنى الراضي فإنه من قنعت به قناعة وقناعا وقنعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Labīd's line uses qanaʿūʿī in the sense associated with satisfaction or contentment.
rows.anchor: وإعطائى المولى على حين فقره ... إذا قال أبصر خلتى وقنوعى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lahum ʿalayya dhanb means they count a fault against me, with ʿalā used in the sense of ʿan; al-Quhayf and Abū al-Najm illustrate the usage.
rows.anchor: مجازه ولهم عندى ذنب قال القحيف العقيلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Quhayf al-ʿUqaylī uses raḍītu ʿalā to mean approval of someone, equivalent to raḍītu ʿannī in this construction.
rows.anchor: إذا رضيت على بنو قشير ... لعمر أبيك أعجمنى رضاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-Najm's woman says he is being accused of a fault he did not commit, illustrating the expression ʿalayya dhanban.
rows.anchor: قد أصبحت أم الخيار تدعى ... على ذنبا كله لم أصنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rasūl here means a message from the Lord of the worlds; ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās and Kathīr ʿAzza provide poetic examples of rasūl for a message.
rows.anchor: مجاره إنا رسالة رب العالمين قال عباس بن مرداس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās uses rasūlan for a message delivered to a household.
rows.anchor: ألا من مبلغ عنى حفافا ... رسولا بيت أهلك منتهاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kathīr ʿAzza uses rasūl to mean a message, in the phrase about not sending a message with a secret.
rows.anchor: لقد كذب الواشون ما بحت عندهم ... بسر ولا أرسلتهم برسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that Pharaoh took the Children of Israel as slaves.
rows.anchor: أي اتخذتهم عبيدا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thʿbān is a moving serpent, while mubīn means visibly clear.
rows.anchor: فإذا هى حية تسعى ثعبانا ومجاز «مبين» أي بين فى الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-qisṭās al-mustaqīm means a just and equitable balance.
rows.anchor: أي بالسواء والعدل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bakhsa means to diminish or deprive someone; the proverb about a supposedly foolish woman who is actually depriving people illustrates the word.
rows.anchor: أي لا تنقصوهم يقال فى المثل: تحسبها حمقاء وهى باخسة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAthā is severe corruption and ruin; the verb is conjugated ʿathaytu, taʿthā, ʿathwan.
rows.anchor: يقال عثيت تعثى عثوا وهى أشد الفساد والخراب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-jibillah means the earlier peoples or creation; its predicate follows the collective sense, and without the final hāʾ its first letter is ḍamma, as in 36:62.
rows.anchor: أي الخلق وجاء خبرها على المعنى الجماع وإذا نزعت الهاء من آخرها ضممت أوله كما هو فى آية أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Dhuʾayb uses al-jabal for a multitude of people in his phrase about the human group, illustrating the collective sense.
rows.anchor: منايا يقربن الحتوف لأهلها ... جهارا ويستمتعن بالأنس الجبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kisaf is plural of kisfa, like sidra and its plural sidr, and means pieces.
rows.anchor: جمع كسفة بمنزلة سدرة والجميع سدر ومعناها قطعا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zubur means the books of earlier peoples; its singular is zabūr.
rows.anchor: أي كتب الأولين واحدها زبور.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿjamī describes a person with a foreign or unclear tongue; ʿajamī refers to someone from non-Arab peoples, not to a linguistic defect.
rows.anchor: يقال رجل أعجم إذا كانت فى لسانه عجمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Animals are called ʿajam because they do not speak; the report “the dumb animal is unaccountable” expresses that no blood-money is due for its harm.
rows.anchor: والدواب عجم لأنها لا تتكلم وجاء فى الحديث العجماء جبار لا تودى أي لادية فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yukaffilūnahu means they take him into their care or include him in their household.
rows.anchor: أي يضمونه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Balagha ashuddahu means he reached maturity; ashudd is plural in sense and has no singular from the same word-form, according to the author.
rows.anchor: بلغ أي انتهى وموضع أشده موضع جميع ولا واحد له من لفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī say the singular of ashudd is shadd, on the faʿl pattern, like baḥr and abḥur.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والكسائي واحد الأشد شد على فعل وأفعل مثل بحر وأبحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istawā means he became fully established and complete.
rows.anchor: أي استحكم وتم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wakaza means he struck him in the chest with his clenched fist; it is a kind of lakz or lahz.
rows.anchor: بمنزلة لهزه فى صدره بجمع كفه، فهو اللكز واللهز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaḍā ʿalayhi means he killed him and finished him off.
rows.anchor: أي فقتله وأتى على نفسه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓahīr means an assisting ally; the source also characterizes him as fearful.
rows.anchor: أي معينا خائفا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yataraqqab means he waits or watches for what is coming.
rows.anchor: أي ينتظر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax means that the man who had asked Moses for help the previous day now cries to Moses for help; istisrākh is calling out for aid.
rows.anchor: مجازه فإذا ذلك الذي كان استنصر هذا يستصرخه أي يستصرخ الذي كان بالأمس استنصره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baṭasha with ṭāʾ kasra or ḍamma are two dialectal forms.
rows.anchor: الطاء مكسورة ومضمومة لغتان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The offspring comes from fluid that is extracted and emitted; mahīn means weak, liquid, and thin. An unnamed poetic line also uses sulālah in this context.
rows.anchor: مجازه ثم خلق ولده من ماء انسل فخرج من مائه أي هراقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited line uses sulālah for the offspring's origin in fluid.
rows.anchor: فجاءت به غضب الأديم غضنفرا ... سلالة فرج كان غير حصين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qalīlan mā tashkurūn means you give thanks little; mā is an extra particle, illustrated by an unnamed poem where it means “after.”
rows.anchor: مجازه: تشكرون قليلا و «ما» من حروف الزوائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍalalnā fī al-arḍ means we have vanished into the earth until no flesh or bone remains.
rows.anchor: مجازه: همدنا فلم يوجد لنا لحم ولا عظم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yatawaffākum is related to counting the dead; Manẓūr al-Zubayrī's line says Quraysh did not count them among the total.
rows.anchor: مجازه من: توفى العدد من الموتى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manẓūr al-Zubayrī uses tawaffā for counting people in the phrase that Quraysh did not count them among the number.
rows.anchor: ولا توفاهم قريش فى العدد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bakratan wa-aṣīlan means the interval from late afternoon until night.
rows.anchor: ما بين العصر إلى الليل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yuṣallī ʿalaykum means “blesses you”; al-Aʿshā's line uses the same verb as evidence.
rows.anchor: عليك مثل الذى صليت فاغتمضى ... نوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The women whose wages are mentioned are those whose dowries the Prophet gave them.
rows.anchor: أي أعطيت مهورهن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fayʾ means what God opened or granted to the Prophet as spoils.
rows.anchor: أي مما فتح الله عليك من الفيء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the conditional expression about a believing woman, the past form wahabat functions as the present subjunctive tahab; Arabic may state one conditional particle while implying the other.
rows.anchor: مجازُه: إن تهب والموضع موضع مجازاة والعرب قد تجازى بحرف وتضمر الآخر معهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-Rumma's line illustrates a conditional construction with an understood counterpart to the stated particle.
rows.anchor: وإنى متى أشرف على الجانب الذي ... به أنت ما بين الجوانب ناظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic may use a past verb where a future or subjunctive is intended in a conditional; the quoted “if they hear” line means “they will fly.”
rows.anchor: وهبت فى موضع «تهب» والعرب تفعل ذلك قال: إن يسمعوا ريبة طاروا بها فرحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic may begin by speaking about someone absent and then address that person directly while still meaning the same addressee.
rows.anchor: والعرب قد تخاطب فتخبر عن الغائب والمعنى للشاهد فترجع إلى الشاهد فتخاطبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAntarah's address to the daughter of Makhram illustrates this shift from reference to an absent person to direct address.
rows.anchor: شطت مزار العاشقين فأصبحت ... عسرا على طلابك ابنة مخرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial hamza is affirmative, informative, and confirmatory, not interrogative; it confirms the idolaters' worship of angels and addresses them with censure.
rows.anchor: مجاز الألف هاهنا مجاز الإيجاب والإخبار والتقرير وليست بألف الاستفهام بل هى تقرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jarīr's “are you not the best” is a rhetorical confirmation, illustrating a hamza that is not a genuine question.
rows.anchor: ألستم خير من ركب المطايا ... وأندى العالمين بطون راح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miʿshār means a tenth of what was given.
rows.anchor: أي عشر ما أعطيناهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nakīr means God's alteration and punishment.
rows.anchor: أي تغييرى وعقوبتى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathnā wa-furādā means two by two and one by one.
rows.anchor: اثنين اثنين وفردا فردا ولا ينون فى مثنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammarians explain the absence of nunation on mathnā as a result of its being diverted from its regular form.
rows.anchor: زعم النحويون لأنه صرف عن وجهه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqdhifu bi-al-ḥaqq means that God brings or sends the truth.
rows.anchor: أي يأتى بالحق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Annā can mean “how” or “where.”
rows.anchor: أي كيف لهم وأين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without hamza, tanāwush derives from n-w-sh and means taking or reaching; Ghaylān's poem uses nawsh for reaching water from above.
rows.anchor: «من نشت تنوش» وهو التناول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With hamza, tanāwush derives from naʾashtu ilayhi and means reaching something from a distance; Ruʾbah's poem illustrates the hamzated form.
rows.anchor: «نأشت إليه» وهو من بعد المطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arāʾik is plural of arīka, a couch inside a curtained chamber; Dhu al-Rumma's verse compares faces to couches.
rows.anchor: واحدتها أريكة وهى الفرش فى الحجال قال ذو الرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā yadʿūn means whatever they desire; Arabic uses “call for” to mean “wish.”
rows.anchor: تقول العرب: ادع على ما شئت أي تمنى على ما شئت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salāmun is nominative with an implied “for them”; qawlan is a verbal noun that does not share the verb's form.
rows.anchor: عملت فيها. و «قولا» خرجت مخرج المصدر الذي يخرج من غير لفظ فعله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imtāzū means separate or distinguish yourselves.
rows.anchor: أي تميزوا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jibillan has a heavy form, while some recite it lighter with a ḍamma on the first letter and a doubled lām; both forms mean creation or a group.
rows.anchor: مثقل وبعضهم لا يثقل ويضم الحرف الأول ويثقل اللام ومعناهن الخلق والجماعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭamasa describes a blind eye with no slit between its lids; the verb also means that wind erases tracks or a person erases writing.
rows.anchor: يقال: أعمى طمس ومطموس وهو أن لا يكون بين جفنى العين غر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same verb is used when wind erases a trace so it cannot be seen, or when someone erases writing.
rows.anchor: والريح تطمس الأثر فلا يرى والرجل يطمس الكتاب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-hdūhum means guide or lead them to the path of Hell; Arabs say a woman was guided to her husband, while some say she was presented to him as a gift.
rows.anchor: تقول العرب: هديت المرأة إلى زوجها أي دللتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mustaslim is one who yields and gives himself up.
rows.anchor: المستسلم الذي يعطى بيديه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means “when they were told, say: There is no god but God,” with an omitted imperative.
rows.anchor: مجازها: إذا قيل لهم: قولوا لا إله إلا الله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception “except God's sincere servants” can follow a general statement as in ordinary Arabic “you are all going except Zayd.”
rows.anchor: تقول العرب: إنكم لذاهبون إلا زيدا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In surur, the first two vowels are ḍamma; some Arabs use fatḥa on the second in similar doubled patterns.
rows.anchor: مضموم الأول والثاني وبعض العرب يفتحون الحرف الثاني من أشباه هذا من باب المضاعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kaʾs is the drinking vessel together with its contents, and maʿīn is pure, flowing water.
rows.anchor: الكأس الإناء بما فيه والمعين الماء الطاهر الجاري.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negation means the drink causes no ghawl; ghawl is what overcomes and destroys the drinkers' reason, as an unnamed poet says of wine.
rows.anchor: مجازه: ليس فيها غول والغول أن تغتال عقولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet's verb taghtālunā describes cups overpowering the drinkers one after another.
rows.anchor: وما زالت الكأس تغتالنا ... وتذهب بالأول الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zumaran means separated groups following one another; its singular is zumrah, and al-Akhṭal uses zumar for a group.
rows.anchor: جماعات فى تفرقة وبعضهم على أثر بعض واحدتها زمرة قال الأخطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence about the God-fearing entering Paradise is left without its result after “when they reached it”; Arabic poetry likewise omits an understood ending.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا جاؤها وفتحت أبوابها وقال لهم خزنتها سلام عليكم طبتم فادخلوها خالدين» (73) مكفوف عن خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbd Manāf ibn Rubʿ al-Hudhalī's final lines illustrate an omitted ending in a conditional construction.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا أسلكوهم فى قتائدة ... شلا كما تطرد الجمالة الشردا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Akhṭal also ends a poem with a clause whose understood completion is omitted.
rows.anchor: خلا إن حيا من قريش تفضلوا ... على الناس أو أن الأكارم نهشلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥāffīn means that the angels surround the Throne on all sides.
rows.anchor: أطافوا به بحفافيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can omit the preposition bāʾ in Qur'anic constructions of this kind.
rows.anchor: والعرب قد تخلى الباء منها فى القرآن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā zāgha al-baṣar means the sight did not deviate or stray.
rows.anchor: ما عدل ولا جار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āyāt means signs, wonders, or marvels of the Lord.
rows.anchor: من أعلام ربه الكبرى وعجائبه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, and Manāt were stone idols inside the Kaʿba that people worshipped.
rows.anchor: أصنام من حجارة كانت فى جوف الكعبة يعبدونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about males and females is an elliptical construction whose expected completion is omitted.
rows.anchor: مجازه: مكفوف عن خبره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍīzā means an unjust, deficient division that deprives someone of a due; ḍāzahu or ḍayazahu means to reduce or withhold his share.
rows.anchor: ناقصة ضرته حقه، وضزته حقه تضيزه وتضوزه تنقصه وتمنعه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says some people hamza the word as aḍaʾaztuhu, with the same sense of depriving someone of a right.
rows.anchor: ربما همزها قوم فقال اضأزته وأنا أضأزه وهى من ضيزى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-lamam is neither indecency nor a major sin; the exception is elliptical and means “unless someone slips into something outside those categories.”
rows.anchor: ليس هو من الفواحش ولا من كبائر الإثم وقد يستثنى الشيء من الشيء وليس منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet's example of a land with no people except gazelles and camels shows that an exception may name something outside the class in the main statement.
rows.anchor: وبلدة ليس بها أنيس ... إلا اليعافير وإلا العيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fuṭūr means cracks or splits.
rows.anchor: «هل ترى من فطور» (3) صدوع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāsiʾ means driven away or rebuffed.
rows.anchor: «خاسئا» (4) مبعدا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥasīr means unable to see; an unnamed early poet uses maḥsūr for the spent or exhausted sight of a camel's eyes.
rows.anchor: فشط ها نظر العينين محسور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manākib means the sides or regions of the earth.
rows.anchor: فى جوانبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamūru describes the earth wavering or moving like a cloud.
rows.anchor: كما يمور السحاب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāffāt are birds spreading their wings, then folding and beating them.
rows.anchor: باسطات أجنحتهن ويقبضن فيضربن بأجنحتهن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qalīlan mā tashkurūn means you give thanks little.
rows.anchor: تشكرون قليلا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zulfah means nearness; the quoted phrase zulfā fa-zulfā illustrates approaching by stages.
rows.anchor: قربة، قال: طى الليالي زلفا فزلفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thing they invoked is what they call upon and then deny or reject.
rows.anchor: أي تدعون به وتكذبون وتردون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghawran means sunken or deep underground; ghawr is a verbal noun used adjectivally, as in Ibn al-Zibaʿrā's use of būr.
rows.anchor: مجازها: غائرا والغور مصدر وقد تفعل العرب ذلك، قال ابن الزبعرى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zibaʿrā's verse uses būr as a verbal noun functioning adjectivally.
rows.anchor: راتق ما فتقت إذ أنا بور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zibaʿrā can describe someone with abundant facial and eyebrow hair, or a shaggy camel.
rows.anchor: والزبعرى كثير شعر الوجه والحاجبين وجمل زبعرى كذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kuw wirat means the sun is wrapped like a turban and then disappears.
rows.anchor: مثل تكوير العمامة، تلف فتمحى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inkadarat means it fell or plunged down; al-ʿAjjāj uses the verb for a falling movement.
rows.anchor: يقال: انكدر فلان انصب، قال العجاج:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mawʾūdah is a daughter buried alive; al-Farazdaq's line praises Saʿṣaʿa ibn Nājiyah, his grandfather, for saving buried girls.
rows.anchor:
قال الفرزدق:
ومنا الذي منع الوائدات ... وأحيا الوئيد فلم يوأد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uzlifat means brought near.
rows.anchor: «وإذا الجنة أزلفت» (13) أدنيت..

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-khunnas, al-jawār, and al-kunnas are the stars.
rows.anchor: هى النجوم.

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One group takes ʿasʿasa as the night bringing on its darkness.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم: إذا أقبلت ظلماؤه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another group takes ʿasʿasa as the night withdrawing or departing.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: إذا ولى ألا تراه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The morning's breathing means dawn begins to emerge; ʿAlqamah ibn Qurṭ's line describes dawn breathing and night withdrawing.
rows.anchor: قال علقمة بن قرط: حتى إذا الصبح لها تنفسا ... وانجاب عنها ليلها وعسعسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With ẓāʾ, ẓanīn means someone accused or suspect.
rows.anchor: «وما هو على الغيب بظنين» (24) أي متهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With ḍād, ḍanīn means someone who is miserly with or withholds it.
rows.anchor: و «بضنين» يضن به ويضن.
